rv.q: It is utterly, pole-axingly beautiful.

Hiddleston excels in a brilliant performance as Robert, the publisher who is cuckolded by the seven-year affair between his wife Emma (Zawe Ashton) and his best friend, literary agent Jerry (Charlie Cox).
It makes a fitting finale to a season that has celebrated Pinter’s ability to express the molten nature of identity and unsettling loneliness of existence.

Period details: the chaps knock back a couple of bottles of wine at lunchtime, and the adulterous couple have a flat in Kilburn because no one goes there; oh, and the woman buys tablecloths and makes stew. None of the emotions is limited by date. More than one person feels betrayed here: friend, lover, partner.
Yet the revelation of this excellent production is its reminder that betrayal is never-ending and that the one deceived forever haunts the imagination.
In moments such as this, Betrayal does illuminate the heart.
Lloyd’s production is exceptionally controlled, nailing every beat, while also bringing out from the text a surprising amount of humour and warmth, finding laughs even in its bleaker moments.
Funny, sharp, oddly nasty, and memorably anguished, Lloyd’s Betrayal is fully faithful to a theatrical landmark.
This sparse, elegant production closes Lloyd's revelatory and handsomely cast season of Pinter's shorter pieces in the theatre that bears the playwright's name.
It is the tall, terrific Zawe Ashton as this cool enchantress who steals the show.
Not that Lloyd’s production here is anything but watchable.
I can confidently say Lloyd's is the most acute, spellbinding, and at times most surprising, I've ever seen.
The Jamie Lloyd Company’s production of Betrayal brings the Pinter at the Pinter season to a triumphant conclusion.
Both quietly radical and faithful to Pinter’s play, Lloyd has revealed “Betrayal” anew.
It is Betrayal as I've never seen it before, and like this entire season, it bathes Pinter in a brilliant new light.
Jamie Lloyd locates the radical soul of a classic work...A searing climax to a thrilling season.

As our three journeyers traverse Pinter’s love-trap, controlling and suppressing their emotions as they go, familial familiarities and the human condition are wryly observed with a mixture of absolute honesty and under-your-nose deceit.
That said, I enjoyed this production because the story, the psychological intricacies and the wonky back-to-front structure are always a source of pleasure.
With its crystalline psychological detail and chic minimal staging, this is by far the best revival of this play that I have ever seen.
Pinter’s dissection of infidelity cuts deep, and this production brings it painfully to life.
It’s a first-rate performance: powerful and wonderfully measured, with its spins of needed humour.

cn.t: Lloyd's stripped-back, stylish production earns widespread acclaim for its spare elegance and star turns, particularly Hiddleston's. Critics praise the director's masterful command of Pinter, though some find the minimalism excessive.
